newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-RIO CLUBS NEAR TO ENDING ROW OVER RULES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RIO CLUBS NEAR TO ENDING ROW OVER RULES.

text.p: Three leading clubs, who boycotted their opening matches in the Rio de Janeiro soccer championship at the weekend because they did not agree with the rules of the competition, appeared on Tuesday to be close to ending the row.

Flamengo, Fluminense and Botafogo, three of the four major teams in the tournament, all refused to take the field on Sunday, saying the rules forced them to play too many games against minor opposition.
As a result, three of the six matches were postponed and Vasco da Gama, the only major club to play, were watched by just 1,600 people as they began with a 3-0 win over Bangu.

On Monday, Flamengo president Kleber Leite called on the club's fans to take part in a protest march in the centre of the city on Friday against the Rio de Janeiro football federation, which organises the competition.

But later in the day, directors appeared ready to agree on a new format for the tournament. "There's been a significant advance," said Flamengo director Michel Assef. Meanwhile, Brazil's national federation, the CBF, watched from afar, refusing to intervene.
The original proposal was for the four major clubs to qualify automatically from the first stage of the tournament, which would have enabled them to field reserve teams.
They would then have played a second state along with the four best of the other teams from the first stage to decide the championship.
The rebellion was sparked by a subsequent change in which the federation's members voted that the tournament would have a final involving the winners of the first and second stages.
This meant the major clubs, who planned to send their first teams to take part in a Rio-Sao Paulo tournament while the first stage was taking place, would have to take the first stage seriously.

Under the proposal made on Monday, the tournament would be halted until early February to enable the major clubs to play their Sao Paulo rivals. It would then be divided into three stages, with the winners of each meeting in a three-way final stage. The results of Sunday's three games would stand.
Brazil is unique among major soccer nations in devoting the first half of the season to regional championships, which are famous for their often eccentric formats.
